titleText.es: Las epidemias de gripe azotan con más fuerza a los adultos jóvenes porque sus sistemas inmunitarios reaccionan con más fuerza, así que para permanecer sanos tenéis que pasaros las próximas semanas borrachos y privados de sueño.
titleText.en: Flu epidemics hit young adults harder because their immune systems react more strongly, so to stay healthy you all have to spend the next few weeks drunk and sleep-deprived.
titleText.noteEn: This translates the Spanish archive text. The official English title text adds that this behavior is meant to keep the immune system ‘suppressed’; that final purpose is absent from the Spanish archive. The joke reverses ordinary health advice by treating a weakened immune response as protection.

cards.answerEn: Use para followed by the verb’s dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir and is called the infinitive. Use para + verb when the same person or thing performs both actions: in estudio para aprender, I both study and learn. When someone else performs the second action, Spanish needs the different pattern para que.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “in order to do something” in Spanish?

example.en: I study in order to learn.

cards.answerEn: Write qué, cómo, cuándo, and similar words with an accent when they ask a question or add an exclamation.
cards.noteEn: This includes direct questions (¿Qué quieres?), questions inside another sentence (No sé qué quiere), and exclamations (¡Qué bonito!). Without the accent, these words usually connect parts of a sentence instead: el libro que quiero means “the book that I want.”
cards.questionEn: Why do words such as que, como, and cuando sometimes have a written accent?

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; helps desarrollarse mean ‘to develop or progress’
cards.noteEn: With a project, plan, or situation as the subject, desarrollarse describes how it unfolds or progresses without naming an outside doer.

example.es: La reunión se desarrolla con calma.

cards.noteEn: Desarrolla is the present form used with one project or situation. With se, it describes that subject unfolding over time.

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.promptEs: gripe porcina · pánico desinformado en Twitter
cards.answerEn: The 2009 H1N1 outbreak was widely called ‘swine flu.’ Twitter's then-new real-time search made it easy to watch rumors, fear, and wildly mistaken self-diagnoses spread alongside genuine news.
cards.noteEn: The strip turns a live search page into a rapid sample of online panic: unrelated injuries, conspiracy claims, and impossible precautions are all attributed to the same outbreak.

cards.answerEn: uninformed; based on poor information (masculine singular)

cards.questionEn: What does gripe porcina mean?
cards.noteEn: Gripe means flu. Porcina means related to pigs and takes its feminine singular form to match the feminine noun gripe.

example.es: El hospital confirmó un caso de gripe porcina.
example.en: The hospital confirmed a case of swine flu.

cards.noteEn: Porcina describes something related to pigs. Its -a ending matches a feminine singular noun such as gripe.

example.es: La granja aplica controles de sanidad porcina.

cards.noteEn: Dios names God, but said by itself it can also react to surprise, excitement, frustration, or strong nostalgia. The tone decides whether natural English keeps ‘God’ or uses an exclamation such as ‘man.’
Cerdo can name the animal or its meat. This card is for the food meaning.
Before a full event with its own verb, antes normally begins the connector antes de que.

cards.promptEs: antes de + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that one action happens before another action by the same person?
cards.answerEn: Use antes de, then keep the second action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir, such as salir, comer, or escribir. Use antes de directly before that form when no new subject is named. If the later action has its own stated subject, Spanish normally uses antes de que and a different verb form.

example.es: Apaga la luz antes de salir.
example.en: Turn off the light before leaving.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links antes to the following action
cards.noteEn: Keep de after antes when the next action stays in its unchanged dictionary form: antes de salir. English expresses the sequence with 'before' and does not translate de separately.

example.es: Lávate las manos antes de comer.

cards.noteEn: After a negative verb, nada is commonly translated as “anything,” even though its basic meaning is “nothing.” Spanish keeps both negative words.

cards.questionEn: What does cinta americana name in Spain?
cards.noteEn: This is a fixed regional name for strong cloth-backed adhesive tape. Other places may prefer cinta adhesiva or cinta de tela.

example.es: Cierra la caja con cinta americana.
example.en: Seal the box with duct tape.

cards.noteEn: Americana ordinarily means ‘American’ in the feminine singular. In Spain, the fixed name cinta americana refers to strong cloth-backed duct tape.

example.en: I need duct tape to fix it.

cards.promptEs: poder + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone can, could, or may do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of poder for the person and situation, then keep the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Poder changes to forms such as puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, and pueden for present ability or possibility. Podría can present a possible or imagined option. The following action keeps its -ar, -er, or -ir ending.
Contra can introduce the danger that a barrier, medicine, or precaution is meant to stop.

example.es: Esta crema protege contra el sol.
example.en: This cream protects against the sun.

cards.answerEn: to get it; to obtain it
cards.noteEn: Conseguir is the unchanged dictionary form ‘to get.’ La is attached to its end and replaces one feminine thing.

example.en: I want to get it today.

cards.promptEs: verbo en forma de diccionario + pronombre unido
cards.questionEn: Where can a short object word such as me, te, lo, or la go with an unchanged action verb?
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the verb and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: An unchanged dictionary-form verb ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Short object words can attach directly: conocer + te becomes conocerte, and ayudar + me becomes ayudarme.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone does one thing without doing another?
cards.answerEn: Put sin before the second action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged verb ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. When the same person performs both actions, Spanish uses sin directly before that form; it does not add a word equivalent to English “-ing.”

example.en: She left without closing the door.

cards.answerEn: to go out; to go outside

cards.questionEn: How do you say how much time someone has left?
cards.answerEn: Put me, te, le, nos, os, or les before quedar, and make quedar singular or plural to match the time amount that remains.
cards.noteEn: Spanish presents the time as remaining to the person. Use queda with one remaining unit and quedan with plural units: me queda una hora, but me quedan dos horas. The small word before quedar identifies who has that time left. You may add a + a name or person to clarify who: A Marta le quedan dos horas.

example.es: A Marta le quedan dos horas.

cards.answerEn: before; until, after an amount of remaining time
cards.noteEn: After an expression such as queda tiempo, para que can introduce the later event that the remaining time leads up to. It does not express a desired purpose in this use.

example.es: Queda una hora para que empiece la película.
example.en: There is one hour left until the film starts.

cards.promptEs: tiempo restante + para que + evento futuro
cards.questionEn: How do you name the later event that a remaining amount of time leads up to?
cards.answerEn: After the remaining-time expression, use para que and put the later event's verb in its special not-yet-a-fact form.
cards.noteEn: That special form is called the subjunctive. It appears because the later event is still ahead: ordinary empieza becomes empiece, and ordinary llega becomes llegue. In this time construction, para que means that the stated time remains before or until the event; it is not giving a purpose.

example.es: Quedan dos horas para que empiece el partido.
example.en: There are two hours left until the match starts.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes the time connector after para
cards.noteEn: Here que joins para to a full later event with its own changed verb.

example.es: Faltan dos días para que llegue Marta.
example.en: There are two days left until Marta arrives.

cards.answerEn: arrives; comes (special form for a future event)
cards.noteEn: Llegue is a form of llegar used after connectors such as cuando or para que when the arrival has not happened yet. The written u keeps the hard g sound before e.

example.en: I will call you when I arrive.

cards.answerEn: belonging to; often expressed with ’s in English
cards.noteEn: De can connect a thing to its owner. Spanish says el libro de Ana where English can say ‘Ana’s book.’

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; Spanish uses the article before a general feminine plural group
cards.noteEn: Spanish often keeps las before a category discussed in general, where English may use a bare plural: las bicicletas, las herramientas.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; Spanish uses the article before a general group
cards.noteEn: Spanish normally uses los before a plural group discussed as a whole, as in los programadores. English often leaves “the” out and simply says “programmers” when making the same general statement.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; marks an “I” verb that is used with me
cards.noteEn: Some Spanish verbs conventionally come with me, te, se, nos, or os even when no one literally acts on themselves. Me marks the speaker's form. English usually absorbs it into the verb's meaning.

cards.answerEn: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?

cards.noteEn: Caído is the completed-action form of caer, ‘to fall.’

cards.answerEn: through; along; down; via (a movement path)
cards.noteEn: Por can mark the path followed during movement. English may choose through, along, down, or via according to the route.

cards.answerEn: marks an action whose doer is not named
cards.noteEn: Before a third-person verb, se can focus on what happens rather than who does it. English often uses a passive form such as ‘is requested’ or ‘have been discovered.’

cards.promptEs: se + verbo en tercera persona (sin nombrar quién actúa)
cards.questionEn: How can Spanish focus on an action or result without naming who does it?
cards.answerEn: Put se before a third-person verb and state what happens; the person doing it can remain unnamed.
cards.noteEn: English often uses a passive form. Spanish may use se with a simple verb or with a completed construction such as se han encontrado. Other uses of se follow different patterns.
Oído is the completed-action form of oír, ‘to hear.’ It keeps the written accent on í and stays unchanged after a form of haber.

example.en: I have never heard that song.

cards.questionEn: How do you add information about a named person or thing using “who,” “that,” or “which”?
cards.answerEn: Put que after the person or thing, then add a verb and the information about it.
cards.noteEn: Que links the added description to the person or thing before it. It does not change for masculine, feminine, singular, or plural nouns. The added part needs a verb: la casa que vimos means “the house that we saw.”

example.es: La casa que vimos es azul.
example.en: The house that we saw is blue.

cards.noteEn: Que connects a noun to information describing it. Depending on the noun, English translates it as “who,” “that,” or “which.”

example.es: La persona que llamó es mi amiga.
example.en: The person who called is my friend.

cards.questionEn: How can Spanish turn an ordinary statement into a yes-or-no question?
cards.answerEn: Use question marks and questioning intonation; Spanish does not need a separate helper like English do or does.
cards.noteEn: The word order can remain the same as in a statement, especially in conversation. The opening and closing question marks show the question in writing.

cards.answerEn: sounds; seems (before a comparison with a)
cards.noteEn: A form of sonar followed by a can compare the impression something gives with another thing.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something sounds like something else?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of sonar, then a, then the thing it resembles.
cards.noteEn: Sonar changes to match the person or thing producing the impression and the time: suena for one present thing, suenan for several. The word a stays unchanged before the comparison.

example.en: That plan sounds like a disaster.

cards.answerEn: like; required after sonar before the comparison
cards.noteEn: In sonar a algo, the preposition a links the impression to what it resembles.

example.en: The story sounds like a joke.

cards.noteEn: Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.noteEn: Hecho is the irregular completed-action form of hacer, “to do” or “to make.” After a form of haber, it corresponds to English “done.”

example.en: I have already done the homework.

cards.noteEn: This card is for the animal, not pork as food.

example.es: El cerdo duerme en el establo.
example.en: The pig sleeps in the barn.

cards.answerEn: The claim that vaccines cause autism is false. Extensive research across large populations has found that vaccines do not cause autism.
cards.noteEn: The comic places that false claim inside a stream of absurd health misinformation. The later action toward an autistic child extends the joke by showing a dangerous conclusion drawn from the same false premise.

cards.answerEn: they are (in a place or state)

cards.questionEn: How do you say that one thing is linked to another?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of estar, then vinculado changed to match the linked thing, then a before the related thing.
cards.noteEn: Estar changes to match the linked person or thing and the time: está for one present item and están for several. Vinculada describes one feminine-noun item, vinculados several masculine or mixed items, and vinculadas several feminine-noun items. The linking word a stays unchanged, but it combines with el as al.

example.es: La cuenta está vinculada al teléfono.
example.en: The account is linked to the phone.

cards.noteEn: Vinculadas describes more than one thing named by a feminine noun. The usual link to the related thing is a.

example.es: Las cuentas están vinculadas al mismo correo.
example.en: The accounts are linked to the same email address.

cards.noteEn: Al is the required contraction of a + el. Spanish writes them as one word whenever both occur together.

cards.answerEn: so; therefore (as part of así que)

cards.questionEn: How do you connect a situation to its result with “so”?
cards.answerEn: Use así que before the result.
cards.noteEn: Así que joins a cause or situation to what follows from it. The two words work together as one connector; translating así and que separately will not give the intended meaning.

example.es: Está lloviendo, así que llevo un paraguas.
example.en: It is raining, so I am carrying an umbrella.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of a result connector
Use a form of estar followed by an action word ending in -ando or -iendo.
cards.noteEn: Estar changes to show who is doing the action: estoy, estás, está, and so on. For most verbs, replace -ar with -ando (hablar → hablando) and replace -er or -ir with -iendo (comer → comiendo, vivir → viviendo). This is similar to English “am/is/are doing.”
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone is in the middle of doing something?

cards.noteEn: Autista has the same singular form with masculine and feminine nouns.
Proteger is the unchanged dictionary form ‘to protect.’ Me attaches to its end and makes the speaker the person protected.

example.en: I use gloves to protect myself.
